subsection: 2. Case study: the 1848 Revolution in Germany

notes.b: The German revolution of 1848 grew out of economic hardship, liberal demands for constitutions and the wish for a united German nation, all set against the settlement of 1815.
points: Poor harvests in 1846 and 1847, with the potato blight from 1845, raised food prices and pushed many workers and peasants into hunger.
An economic depression in 1847 closed businesses, increased unemployment and fuelled urban unrest across the German states.
Liberals wanted constitutions, freedom of the press and assembly, trial by jury and a national parliament, most of which the Confederation's governments had refused.
Nationalists wanted a German nation state, but disagreed on whether it should include the German-speaking lands of the Habsburg Empire.
News of the February Revolution in Paris (22–24 February 1848), which ended the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe, encouraged German liberals to press their demands.
Liberal opposition in the states had already been building through the Diets and the press, notably in Baden, Württemberg, Bavaria and Saxony.

notes.b: Within weeks of the Paris revolution, rulers across the German states conceded liberal demands to avoid being overthrown.
points: In Baden, the liberal leaders Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve led a republican rising in April 1848, but Baden's troops defeated it at Kandern.
In Berlin on 18 March 1848, fighting broke out between citizens and Prussian troops, and barricades were erected in the city.
Frederick William IV of Prussia withdrew the troops, promised a constitution and a German national assembly, and on 21 March rode through Berlin to honour the dead of the fighting.
Across the states, rulers appointed liberal ministers, promised constitutions and freedom of the press, and allowed armed citizens' militias.
Governments in Hanover and Saxony accepted liberal ministries under pressure from crowds.
The March concessions created a moment of unity, with liberals of different regions and social classes working together.

notes.h: The Vorparlament and the Frankfurt National Assembly
points: The Vorparlament (preliminary parliament) met in Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April 1848, with elected and self-appointed members from across the German states.
It decided that a national assembly should be elected by universal male suffrage to draw up a constitution for a united Germany.
Elections in April and May 1848 chose about 800 members of the Frankfurt National Assembly, most of them professional men such as lawyers, professors, judges and civil servants.
The Assembly opened on 18 May 1848 in the Paulskirche (St Paul's Church) in Frankfurt.
The Assembly elected the Archduke John of Austria as Reichsverweser (imperial regent) on 29 June 1848, and he formed a provisional central government.
Its president was Heinrich von Gagern, a moderate liberal from Hesse, who favoured a German state under Prussian leadership.
The Assembly had no army or revenue of its own and depended on the states to enforce its decisions.

notes.h: Debates: Grossdeutsch or Kleindeutsch, and the Basic Rights
points: The Grossdeutsch (Greater German) solution would include all German-speaking lands, including the Austrian Habsburg lands, in a single state.
The Kleindeutsch (Lesser German) solution would unite the German states under Prussia and exclude Austria, which was linked to non-German peoples.
The Assembly debated the question for months, and the choice of Kleindeutsch in the end meant a Germany without the Habsburg lands.
The Basic Rights of the German People, approved in December 1848, promised freedom of the press, assembly, religion and association, and equality before the law.
The Basic Rights abolished noble privileges and feudal dues, and they guaranteed trial by jury and the right to a legal defence.
The Assembly's draft constitution (1849) established a two-chamber parliament, with an elected lower house and a federal upper house.
Schleswig-Holstein was ruled by the Danish king, but its German-speaking population wanted to join the German Confederation.
In March 1848 the duchies rose against Denmark, and Prussian troops intervened to support them.
Under pressure from Britain and Russia, Prussia agreed to the Malmö armistice in August 1848, which abandoned the duchies' cause.
The Frankfurt Assembly accepted the armistice, which angered radicals and led to street violence in Frankfurt in September 1848.
Two conservative members, Prince Felix Lichnowsky and General Hans von Auerswald, were murdered by a crowd in Frankfurt on 18 September 1848.
The Schleswig-Holstein question remained unresolved and the war with Denmark continued until 1851.

notes.b: By late 1848 the old governments had regained control of the main centres through force, and the liberals in the German states lost their momentum.
points: In June 1848 the Austrian general Windischgrätz bombarded and took Prague, ending the Czech national rising.
In Vienna, a radical uprising in October 1848 led to fighting, and Windischgrätz recaptured the city on 31 October 1848.
The Saxon radical Robert Blum, who had sat in the Frankfurt Assembly, was executed in Vienna on 9 November 1848.
In Berlin, Frederick William IV appointed a conservative ministry under Count Brandenburg, and troops under General Wrangel entered the city in November 1848.
On 5 December 1848 the king granted Prussia a constitution by decree, with a two-chamber parliament and voting rights tied to tax payments.
The Prussian National Assembly was dissolved at the same time, showing that the king would rule by his own authority.

notes.h: The imperial constitution and the refused crown, 1849
points: The Frankfurt Assembly completed its constitution on 27 March 1849, and offered the hereditary title of German Emperor to Frederick William IV of Prussia.
Frederick William refused the crown on 28 April 1849, saying he would not accept a crown from an assembly of the people, and he rejected the constitution.
The refusal meant that the constitution could not take effect, because most German rulers followed Prussia's lead in rejecting it.
Austria rejected the constitution outright because it excluded the Habsburg lands, and the Austrian government recalled its delegates from Frankfurt.
Several states, including Saxony, Hanover and Bavaria, also refused to accept the constitution.

notes.h: The rump parliament, the risings of 1849 and the Erfurt Union and Olmütz
points: After the refusal, the remaining members of the Frankfurt Assembly moved to Stuttgart, where they were called the rump parliament.
In May 1849 insurgents in Dresden seized the city and in the Palatinate and Baden risings demanded the constitution be implemented.
Prussian and other state troops crushed the risings, and the rump parliament was dispersed by Württemberg troops in June 1849.
Hecker and other radicals fled into exile, and many of the revolutionaries were imprisoned or emigrated to the United States.
Prussia tried to build a smaller German union, the Erfurt Union, in 1850, but Austria and the other states opposed it and the plan collapsed.
The Erfurt Parliament met in March 1850 and was a Prussian-led attempt to reconstitute German unity without Austria.
The Olmütz Agreement (November 1850) forced Prussia to abandon the Erfurt Union and accept the restoration of the German Confederation.
The old German Diet was restored at Frankfurt in 1851, with Austria again presiding, and Bismarck was appointed the Prussian delegate to it in 1851.
The revolution left the liberals discredited, and conservatives used the defeat to strengthen the authority of the monarchies.
The liberals in Frankfurt spent months debating a constitution while the governments rebuilt their forces and their authority.
The Assembly was divided between Grossdeutsch and Kleindeutsch supporters, and this split prevented agreement on the constitution's scope.
The army and the bureaucracy remained loyal to the rulers, and the monarchs were prepared to use force to restore order.
Austria and Prussia recovered their military strength in late 1848 and used it to crush revolts in Vienna, Prague and Berlin.
The revolutionaries lacked the support of the peasants, who were given limited reforms in 1848 and so had less reason to join the cause.
Frederick William IV's refusal of the crown removed the chance of a German state led by a liberal constitution.

notes.b: Contemporaries and later historians disagree on whether 1848 was a failure, a turning point or a necessary stage in German unification.
points: Liberals and radicals at the time saw 1848 as a missed chance, and many of them later accepted Prussian leadership of unification.
Conservative contemporaries praised the restoration of order and the rejection of revolutionary demands.
Historians who stress continuity argue that the revolution's failure paved the way for Bismarck's unification through force.
Historians who stress the achievements point to the Basic Rights, the elections to a national assembly and the abolition of feudal dues as lasting gains.
Assessment: the revolution achieved a great deal on paper and in the March concessions, but its lack of an army, its divisions and the refusal of the crown meant that its aims were not realised.

keyTerms.definition: The elected parliament that met in the Paulskirche at Frankfurt from May 1848 to draw up a constitution for a united Germany.
The preliminary parliament that met at Frankfurt in April 1848 and organised elections to the National Assembly.
The solution to German unity that would include the German-speaking Habsburg lands within a single German state.
The solution to German unity that would unite the German states under Prussia and exclude Austria.
The guarantees of civil liberties approved by the Frankfurt Assembly in December 1848, including freedom of the press and equality before the law.
The remnant of the Frankfurt Assembly that continued to meet at Stuttgart after the refusal of the crown until it was dispersed in June 1849.
Prussia's 1850 plan to unite the German states under its leadership without Austria, which collapsed after Austrian opposition.
The November 1850 agreement that forced Prussia to abandon the Erfurt Union and restored the German Confederation.
The title of imperial regent, given to the Archduke John of Austria by the Frankfurt Assembly in June 1848 to head a provisional central government.
The August 1848 truce between Prussia and Denmark over Schleswig-Holstein, which abandoned the duchies' rising and angered radicals.
